cvrr 0.1.0
  • Get started
  • Reference

Experimental. From a list of CVR numbers to analysable accounting data, in one package: search Erhvervsstyrelsens distribution service, download what it found, and parse the machine-readable filings. Danish and Greenlandic companies alike — Greenland’s own register was folded into CVR in 2018, and its companies file under the same taxonomy. Split out of daos, and named for the functions it has always been made of.

Installation 

pak::pak("dataniel/cvrr")

The whole route 

library(cvrr)

cvr_query(
  cvr          = c("12345678", "87654321"),
  enddate_from = "2020-01-01",
  enddate_to   = "2024-12-31"
) |>
  cvr_search(contact = "you@example.com") |>
  cvr_hits() |>
  cvr_download("materiale/xbrl")

# a whole directory, taxonomy and all
x <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl")

a <- xbrl_accounts(x)
a$company           # who the company is
a$location          # where it is
a$audit             # who audited it, who filed it, with what tool
a$checks            # whether any of it adds up
a$income_statement  # lines, in statement order
a$balance           # lines, with the ones the filer left out derived
a$cash_flow         # the cash flow statement, as reported
a$movements         # the fixed asset note, movement by movement
a$prose             # what management wrote

Four functions to find and fetch, one to read, one to divide up. Nothing in between is manual: no numeric conversion, no period argument, no binding the filings together by hand.

Every table opens with the same key — cvr, name, period_start, period_end — and ends with file, so moving between them needs no looking and every figure can be traced back to the document it came from. The three statements carry reconciled on every row, so filtering to the lines that add up needs no join, and checks gathers the per-filing verdicts in one place.

Validate once, use many times

Screening, the panel and the reports all need the same work done first: the tagging put right, the three statements checked and solved line by line. xbrl_validate() does it once and attaches it to the facts, and every later step reads it instead of doing it again:

v <- read_xbrl("materiale/xbrl") |>
  xbrl_validate()
s <- xbrl_screen(v)
p <- xbrl_panel(v)
xbrl_report(v, "12345678.html", cvr = "12345678", peers = p)

The result is still the facts, not a panel. A panel keeps a few dozen variables per company and year and drops the rest: the notes and the dimensions, the lines beyond its variables, and where each figure came from. A subset of whole filings (v[v$cvr == "12345678", ]) keeps the work. Each filing is fingerprinted, so a figure changed after validation is never read from stale work. That filing is simply done again.

A panel to analyse

xbrl_panel() turns the filings into one row per company and year, with the statement figures as named variables (revenue, gross_profit, operating_profit, profit, assets, equity, cash, cf_operating, …) beside the company’s background and how far its figures can be trusted. A company’s time series and a cross-section of many companies are the same table:

p <- xbrl_panel(x)
p[p$cvr == "12345678", c("period_end", "gross_profit", "operating_profit", "equity")]

It is built from the statements as xbrl_lines() gives them, after the tagging has been put right. One sign convention holds throughout: costs are positive amounts, a loss is negative, and tax is signed by the two results on either side of it. A figure the filing does not report is NA and never an estimate. Most class B filings start at the gross profit, so revenue is there for 13% of the corpus and gross_profit for 97%. In 99.9% of rows the assets equal equity, provisions and debt.

Ratios, and how robust a company is

xbrl_ratios() adds the ratios statistics offices publish, the change from the previous year, and each company’s place among comparable companies the same year. xbrl_robustness() adds the signs of financial vulnerability: negative equity, capital lost, thin equity, two losses, heavy short-term debt, weak interest cover, a return well under peers, youth, and a going concern uncertainty. It also says how far the gross profit could fall before the operating profit is gone, and how many months of wages the cash covers:

r <- xbrl_robustness(xbrl_panel(x))
r[r$n_factors >= 3, c("cvr", "name", "period_end", "n_factors")]

The factors are held against the data. A company that files no annual report in the next two years has most often ceased. With weak interest cover, capital lost or a weak return that happened 2.6-2.7 times as often as without, and with four or more factors 13.5% of the time against 4.8% with none. A branch of industry is the better comparison group, but it is not in a filing. Join it from a register extract and pass group = "branch".

A report

xbrl_report() runs the whole chain (standardise, screen, panel, ratios, robustness) and writes one self-contained HTML page. The data decides which report it is: one company in one year, one company over time, many companies in one year, or many over time. type overrides that. The page opens with what matters most, in sentences, and has the tables behind them underneath:

xbrl_report(x, "12345678.html", cvr = "12345678", peers = xbrl_panel(x))
xbrl_report(x, "all.html")

The content is also there as data. xbrl_report_data() returns the tables and the sentences, so a report of one’s own can be built from the same parts. The page needs nothing outside R, no pandoc and no internet. It is in Danish by default, and lang = "en" gives English.

Which filings are worth reading?

xbrl_screen() runs every check over a pile of filings and returns what they found, one row per finding, ranked by how much it would change what a reader takes from the accounts:

s <- xbrl_screen(x)
s[s$severity == "high", ]

The checks cover an auditor’s qualified, adverse or missing opinion and a going concern uncertainty, a balance sheet that does not balance, an income statement step no signs explain, a cash flow statement that does not add up or reports borrowing the balance sheet does not owe, and balances that reopen on a different amount in the next year’s filing. Each finding carries its amount and its share of total assets, so a rounding difference at a large company does not outrank a real gap at a small one.

The tagging is put right before the accounts are screened. xbrl_standardise() finds figures tagged in thousands where the filing is in kroner and puts them back. It also reverses a cash flow sign where the activity adds up only that way. A sign the activity adds up with is left alone, because then it means something. It keeps the figure as tagged beside the corrected one. Without that step, 41 of the 54 serious findings over 4,304 Danish and Greenlandic filings for 2020-2024 were such figures. With it, 147 figures and 17 signs are corrected first. Then 618 filings have a finding and 93 a serious one. The serious findings are 81 auditor’s opinions that are qualified, adverse or missing, and 13 cash flow statements that do not add up. Each finding carries the filing’s background (accounting class, legal form, level of assurance, part of a group or not), so like can be compared with like.

A finding is a reason to read the report, not a conclusion about it.

A cash flow statement that adds up, and is still wrong

Greenland Airports’ 2025 group accounts reported a DKK 400 million state grant as new long-term borrowing. Every total in the cash flow statement still added up, because moving an amount between activities leaves the totals alone. check_cashflow() holds the statement against the balance sheet, the income statement and the fixed asset note, and on that filing it finds 364 million of borrowing the balance sheet does not owe. It also names the line in investing that takes the same amount back out: a grant taken to income, tagged in the XBRL as SaleOfOtherCompany.

cf <- check_cashflow(x)
cf[cf$verdict == "borrowed more than owed", ]

Two forms, one of them useful

A filing usually exists as both a PDF and an XML file. The XML is XBRL — the machine-readable form — and read_xbrl() turns it into a tibble with one row per reported fact: its value, its context dates, its unit, the namespace that identifies it in the taxonomy, and every dimension the context carries, ConsolidatedSoloDimension included.

The PDF is the human-readable version, and there is no parser for it here. For older filings, small companies, and reports that are a scan of paper, the PDF is the only digital trace, and turning one back into a table is a different kind of work. That is what taxmill is for.

Signs

XBRL amounts often arrive without a meaningful sign: costs can be reported as positive numbers, and the convention varies between preparers. find_signs() recovers them, because an income statement has to reconcile — it searches for the +1/-1/0 assignment that makes the line items sum to the reported total.

find_signs(income, elementid, value,
           total_label = "ProfitLoss",
           by = c(cvr, period_end))

Nothing is dropped: every row comes back with a status of unique, ambiguous, unsolved, no_total or duplicate_total, and items that every candidate assignment agreed on are filled in even when the group as a whole is ambiguous.

The search is tested against an exhaustive one, every assignment enumerated, on random cases from kroner to a group’s hundred billion. That test found a precision fault that turned unique answers ambiguous on large amounts, and the fault is fixed. There is no official answer to check it against. In 13 versions of the Danish taxonomy, 2010-2025, the only calculation linkbase is a 2020 income statement for one kind of education institution. Erhvervsstyrelsen publishes no weights for the ordinary statements. What the taxonomy does publish is each line’s debit or credit marking, and on 8,633 solved income statement lines the recovered sign agrees with it 99.8% of the time.

The taxonomy is where the meaning lives

An XBRL instance carries facts and no readable text at all: labels, the statement hierarchy and the debit/credit markings are in the taxonomy the filing names in one schemaRef. Point read_taxonomy() at the package Erhvervsstyrelsen publishes and the rest follows.

tax  <- read_taxonomy("XBRL20241001.zip")
tidy <- read_xbrl("data/xml/13645183_2024-12-31.xml") |>
  add_taxonomy(tax)

check_statement(tidy)

Every figure arrives with a stable accounting code from the taxonomy’s own numbering, its Danish label, whether it is debit or credit, and — decided by the taxonomy’s declared dimension default rather than by guesswork — whether it is the group’s figure or the parent company’s.

Using the service well

cvr_search() requires a contact email address and sends it as the User-Agent header: Erhvervsstyrelsen asks requests to identify their sender. The function refuses an empty contact, but it cannot check that the address is honest — that part is yours. vignette("cvrr") covers the rest of the habits worth having: query volume, scroll for complete results, testing small first, and the legal frame around reklamebeskyttelse.

Functions

In the order the route runs.

Find and fetch

Function Description
clean_cvr() Standardise CVR numbers to 8 digits: strip a DK prefix, spaces and dashes
cvr_query() Build an Elasticsearch query for published annual reports
cvr_search() Send a query to Erhvervsstyrelsens distribution service
cvr_hits() Flatten a response into a tibble, one row per document
cvr_download() Download the documents found by a search

Read, and divide up

Function Description
read_xbrl() Read one filing, a list of them, or a directory, into one tibble with the taxonomy on it
xbrl_accounts() The filings divided into nine keyed tables: the company, where it is, the audit trail, the checks, the three statements, the fixed asset note and the prose
xbrl_validate() Standardise and check the filings once, and carry the work to every later step
xbrl_panel() One row per company and year: the statement figures as named variables, background and trust columns
xbrl_ratios() Key ratios, the change from last year, and the place among peers
xbrl_robustness() Signs of financial vulnerability, held against which companies stopped filing, and what the figures could absorb
xbrl_report_data() What a report should say, as tables and sentences, for one company or many, one year or several
xbrl_report() The report as one self-contained HTML page
xbrl_company() The company behind a filing: identity, legal form, class, group, auditor and opinion, going concern, employees, activity
xbrl_lines() One statement, line by line, in statement order
xbrl_movements() The fixed asset note as a roll-forward: cost, depreciation and revaluation at each end of the year, and the movements between

Name and place the facts

Function Description
add_taxonomy() Give a filing’s facts their statement, code, label and sign convention
read_taxonomy() Open a taxonomy package and read its catalog, labels and defaults
cvrr_line, cvrr_entry Twelve taxonomies as tables, so no package is needed on disk
xbrl_fill() Derive the subtotals and components a filing left out
xbrl_resolve() Choose between two figures reported for the same line
xbrl_period() Read the accounting period a filing declares for itself
xbrl_note_tables() Read the tables inside a filing’s text notes

Does it add up?

Function Description
xbrl_screen() Every check over a pile of filings, findings ranked by how much they matter
xbrl_standardise() Put the tagging right before screening: figures in the wrong unit, cash flow signs the wrong way
check_statement() Reconcile every subtotal against the lines below it
check_cascade() Reconcile an income statement step by step to the result for the year
check_cashflow() Reconcile a cash flow statement, and tie it to the balance sheet, the income statement and the fixed asset note
check_breakdown() Reconcile a dimensional breakdown against the line it breaks down
check_movement() Reconcile an opening balance and its movements to the closing balance
check_continuity() Does the balance a company closed on reopen in the next filing?
check_inclusion() Find lines a note says are contained in another
find_signs() Recover the signs that reconcile line items to a total

Where the package stops

cvrr hands out the accounting figures the filings actually carry, with the label, the code and the sign convention the taxonomy gives them. Mapping those onto a particular statistic’s variable definitions is yours to make: which element counts as turnover depends on the definitions in force, and a package that decided it for you would be wrong the year they changed.
